claim: Regulatory T cells (Tregs) are essential for maintaining immune tolerance in both lymphoid and non-lymphoid tissues.
source: Regulatory T cells (Tregs) are essential for maintaining immune tolerance in both lymphoid and non-lymphoid tissues.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus about Treg function.

claim: Layilin is predominantly expressed on Tregs in skin.
source: We discovered that layilin, a C-type lectin receptor, is predominantly expressed on Tregs in skin.
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data presented in Figure 1A-C showing LAYILIN expression patterns.

claim: Layilin was highly expressed on a subset of clonally expanded 'effector' Tregs in both healthy and psoriatic human skin.
source: Layilin was highly expressed on a subset of clonally expanded 'effector' Tregs in both healthy and psoriatic human skin.
evidence: Supported by TCR repertoire analysis showing expanded clones in LAYN-expressing Tregs (Figure 1I and J).

claim: Layilin-expressing Tregs exhibited a transcriptional profile indicative of enhanced adhesion.
source: Layilin-expressing Tregs exhibited a transcriptional profile indicative of enhanced adhesion.
evidence: Supported by differential gene expression analysis showing enrichment of adhesion molecules in LAYN-expressing Tregs (Figure 1G-H).

claim: Deletion of layilin in Tregs in mice in vivo resulted in significantly attenuated skin inflammation.
source: Deletion of layilin in Tregs in mice in vivo resulted in significantly attenuated skin inflammation.
evidence: Supported by IMQ model data showing reduced clinical scores in Foxp3Cre/Laynfl/fl mice (Figure 3B-C).

claim: Layilin enhanced in vitro human Treg adhesion via modulation of lymphocyte function-associated antigen-1.
source: Mechanistically, layilin enhanced in vitro human Treg adhesion via modulation of lymphocyte function-associated antigen-1, resulting in distinct cytoskeletal alterations consistent with enhanced focal adhesion and lamellipodia formation.
evidence: Supported by LFA-1 activation assays and adhesion assays (Figure 4D-F).

claim: Layilin modulates Treg motility and adhesion in non-lymphoid tissue.
source: Taken together, we define layilin as a critical regulator of Treg-suppressive capacity by modulating motility and adhesion in a non-lymphoid tissue.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental approaches including in vivo deletion studies, adhesion assays, and cytoskeletal analysis.

claim: Specialized subsets of Tregs stably reside in non-lymphoid tissues, including skin, gut, and lung.
source: Although present in lymphoid organs, specialized subsets of these cells stably reside in non-lymphoid tissues, including skin, gut, and lung (Muñoz-Rojas and Mathis, 2021; Ali and Rosenblum, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Subsets of Tregs in skin play a crucial role in suppressing hair follicle autoreactivity.
source: Subsets of Tregs in skin play a crucial role in suppressing hair follicle autoreactivity (Cohen et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Tregs facilitate hair follicle cycling.
source: In addition, these cells facilitate hair follicle cycling (Ali et al., 2017), augment wound healing (Nosbaum et al., 2016), and establish and maintain tolerance to skin commensals (Scharschmidt et al., 2015; Scharschmidt et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Tregs augment wound healing.
source: In addition, these cells facilitate hair follicle cycling (Ali et al., 2017), augment wound healing (Nosbaum et al., 2016), and establish and maintain tolerance to skin commensals (Scharschmidt et al., 2015; Scharschmidt et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Tregs establish and maintain tolerance to skin commensals.
source: In addition, these cells facilitate hair follicle cycling (Ali et al., 2017), augment wound healing (Nosbaum et al., 2016), and establish and maintain tolerance to skin commensals (Scharschmidt et al., 2015; Scharschmidt et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Layilin is a cell surface C-type lectin receptor.
source: Layilin is a cell surface C-type lectin receptor (Borowsky and Hynes, 1998; Bono et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: C-type lectin receptors play a role in many cellular functions, including adhesion and cell signaling.
source: This family of receptors plays a role in many cellular functions, including adhesion and cell signaling (Brown et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Layilin is preferentially expressed on exhausted CD8+ T cells infiltrating human and murine tumors.
source: Previously, we and others have shown that layilin is preferentially expressed on exhausted CD8+ T cells infiltrating human and murine tumors (Zheng et al., 2017; Fu et al., 2014; Mahuron et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Intratumoral Tregs express high levels of layilin.
source: In addition, intratumoral Tregs express high levels of layilin (Bhairavabhotla et al., 2016; Mehta et al., 2021; De Simone et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Layilin functions to anchor Tregs in non-lymphoid tissues and limits their suppressive capacity.
source: Mechanistically, we have shown that layilin functions to anchor Tregs in non-lymphoid tissues, and in doing so, limits their suppressive capacity (Mehta et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: On CD8+ T cells, layilin co-localizes with integrin αLβ2 (lymphocyte function-associated antigen-1 [LFA-1]), enhancing its adhesive properties.
source: On CD8+ T cells, layilin co-localizes with integrin αLβ2 (lymphocyte function-associated antigen-1 [LFA-1]), enhancing its adhesive properties (Mahuron et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The main population expressing LAYILIN in skin are Tregs.
source: Consistent with previous observations (Bhairavabhotla et al., 2016), the main population expressing LAYILIN are Tregs (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1A-C and consistent with previous literature.

claim: There were no changes in the relative expression of LAYN per cell when comparing Treg clusters from psoriasis skin with healthy control skin.
source: There were no changes in the relative expression of LAYN per cell when comparing Treg clusters from psoriasis skin with healthy control skin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that LAYN expression is not increased on Tregs in inflamed skin.
evidence: Supported by volcano plot analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: LAYN expression is not increased on Tregs in inflamed skin.
source: There were no changes in the relative expression of LAYN per cell when comparing Treg clusters from psoriasis skin with healthy control skin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that LAYN expression is not increased on Tregs in inflamed skin.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that LAYN expression per cell does not change between healthy and psoriatic skin.

claim: Layilin is expressed on ~40–50% of Tregs in both healthy and inflamed skin.
source: Because layilin is expressed on ~40–50% of Tregs in both healthy and inflamed skin (Mehta et al., 2021), we sought to understand how layilin-expressing Tregs differed from layilin-non-expressing Tregs at the transcriptional level.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: LAYN-expressing and non-expressing Tregs have equivalent levels of FOXP3 and CTLA-4 expression.
source: We found that LAYN-expressing (LAYN>0) and non-expressing (LAYN<0) cells are relatively similar to equivalent levels of FOXP3 and CTLA-4 expression (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by violin plot data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: 636 genes were significantly differentially expressed between LAYN-positive and LAYN-negative Tregs in psoriatic skin.
source: Focusing on psoriatic skin, we found that 636 genes were significantly differentially expressed (DEGs) between LAYN-positive and LAYN-negative Tregs (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by volcano plot analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Several TNFRSF family genes and several adhesion molecules, including integrin coding genes (ITGB7 and ITGB6) or cell–cell adhesion (CADM1), were expressed at significantly higher levels in LAYN-expressing Tregs.
source: Interestingly, several TNFRSF family genes and several adhesion molecules, including integrin coding genes (ITGB7 and ITGB6) or cell–cell adhesion (CADM1), were expressed at significantly higher levels in LAYN-expressing Tregs (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Pathways for T cell activation and cell migration and adhesion are enriched in LAYN-expressing Tregs.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) on DEGs revealed pathways for T cell activation and cell migration and adhesion to be enriched in LAYN-expressing Tregs (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: TCR engagement is a potent inducer of layilin expression on Tregs.
source: T cell receptor (TCR) engagement is a potent inducer of layilin expression on Tregs (Mehta et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: LAYN-expressing Tregs had more expanded clones, with the top 15 expressed clonotypes being more abundant in LAYN-expressing cells.
source: Interestingly, LAYN-expressing Tregs had more expanded clones, with the top 15 expressed clonotypes being more abundant in LAYN-expressing cells.
evidence: Supported by TCR repertoire analysis shown in Figure 1I and J.

claim: The clonal expansion pattern in LAYN-expressing Tregs is similar to previous observations made in CD8+ T cells.
source: These findings are similar to previous observations made in CD8+ T cells (Mahuron et al., 2020).
evidence: Comparison to previous literature findings.

claim: LAYN expression correlates with more activated, more motile, and clonally expanded Tregs in psoriatic skin.
source: Taken together, transcriptional immunophenotyping of Tregs isolated from psoriatic skin suggests that LAYN expression correlates with more activated, more motile, and clonally expanded cells.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from multiple data types including transcriptional profiling and TCR analysis.

claim: Deleting layilin on 30–50% of Tregs had no effect on their ability to suppress either CD4+ or CD8+ T cell proliferation in vitro.
source: In these experiments, deleting layilin on 30–50% of Tregs had no effect on their ability to suppress either CD4+ or CD8+ T cell proliferation (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by in vitro suppression assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Deletion of layilin did not influence Treg activation across multiple donors with or without TCR stimulation in vitro.
source: In these experiments, deletion of layilin did not influence Treg activation across multiple donors with or without TCR stimulation (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by spectral flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Layilin plays a minimal role in Treg activation and suppressive capacity in vitro.
source: Taken together, this data suggests that layilin plays a minimal role, if any, in Treg activation and suppressive capacity in vitro.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the in vitro experimental data showing no significant effects.

claim: Layilin acts to anchor Tregs in tissues and deletion selectively in these cells results in enhanced tumor growth.
source: We have previously shown that layilin acts to anchor Tregs in tissues and that deletion selectively in these cells results in enhanced tumor growth (Mehta et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Tregs play a significant role in the imiquimod (IMQ) model of skin inflammation.
source: To test this hypothesis, we utilized the well-established imiquimod (IMQ) model of skin inflammation (Gangwar et al., 2022; van der Fits et al., 2009), where Tregs are known to play a significant role (Choi et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2022; Hartwig et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Foxp3Cre/Laynfl/fl mice showed a significant reduction in Layn expression in Tregs after tamoxifen treatment.
source: These experiments confirmed a significant reduction in Layn expression in Tregs from Foxp3Cre/Laynfl/fl mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Foxp3Cre/Laynfl/fl mice had a significant reduction in the clinical severity of skin inflammation compared to control mice in the IMQ model.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, we observed a significant reduction in the clinical severity of skin inflammation in Foxp3Cre/Laynfl/fl mice treated with tamoxifen compared to age- and gender-matched littermate Foxp3Cre control mice treated with tamoxifen (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Supported by clinical scoring data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Foxp3Cre/Laynfl/fl mice had a significant reduction in the absolute number of skin infiltrating CD4+ Teff cells and CD8+ T cells compared to controls.
source: Foxp3Cre/Laynfl/fl mice had a significant reduction in the absolute number of skin infiltrating CD4+ Teff cells and CD8+ T cells compared to controls (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry quantification shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There was a significant reduction in the number of TNFa-producing CD4+ Teff cells, IL-17-producing CD8+ T cells, and IL-17-producing Tregs in Foxp3Cre/Laynfl/fl mice compared to controls.
source: In addition, there was a significant reduction in the number of TNFa-producing CD4+ Teff cells, IL-17-producing CD8+ T cells, and IL-17-producing Tregs in Foxp3Cre/Laynfl/fl mice compared to controls (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There were no significant differences in the expression of select Treg activation markers between layilin-deleted and control Tregs in the IMQ model.
source: There were no significant differences in the expression of select Treg activation markers between layilin-deleted and control Tregs (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Bulk RNA sequencing identified several differentially expressed genes in Foxp3Cre/Laynfl/fl Tregs relative to Foxp3Cre control Tregs after 4 days of IMQ treatment.
source: These experiments identified several DEGs in Foxp3Cre/Laynfl/fl mice relative to Foxp3Cre control mice both treated with tamoxifen (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: GSEA of DEGs from Tregs in the IMQ model revealed enrichment in pathways involved in cellular movement, locomotion, and migration.
source: Interestingly, GSEA of DEGs revealed enrichment in pathways involved in cellular movement, locomotion, and migration (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Layilin attenuates Treg suppression in vivo without altering their activation capacity.
source: Taken together, these results reveal that layilin attenuates Treg suppression in vivo without altering their activation capacity and is consistent with previous studies that suggest that the anchoring function of layilin limits Treg's ability to optimally mediate immune regulation in skin (Mehta et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the in vivo IMQ model data and consistent with previous literature.

claim: Layilin co-localizes with LFA-1 on CD8+ T cells and functions to augment LFA-1-mediated adhesion of these cells.
source: We have previously shown that layilin co-localizes with LFA-1 on CD8+ T cells and functions to augment LFA-1-mediated adhesion of these cells (Mahuron et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Several genes involved in cellular locomotion, migration, and adhesion were differentially expressed in layilin-expressing vs. layilin-edited human Tregs.
source: Consistent with the experiments described above where layilin was deleted in Tregs in vivo in mice (Figure 3), several genes involved in cellular locomotion, migration, and adhesion were differentially expressed in layilin-expressing vs. layilin-edited cells (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by bulk RNA-seq data from CRISPR-edited human Tregs shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: LFA-1 is critical for the development and function of Tregs.
source: LFA-1 is critical for the development and function of Tregs (Marski et al., 2005; Wohler et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: LFA-1 is present either in a low-affinity inactive form or a high-affinity active form.
source: LFA-1 is present either in a low-affinity inactive form or a high-affinity active form (Sun et al., 2019; Kondo et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In its active form, LFA-1 mediates binding to intercellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM-1) and cell–cell adhesion.
source: In its active form, LFA-1 mediates binding to intercellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM-1) and cell–cell adhesion (Abram and Lowell, 2009; Walling and Kim, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Crosslinking layilin on Tregs resulted in increased LFA-1 activation, as measured by increased m-24 mAb staining.
source: Both in non-stimulated and stimulated conditions, crosslinking layilin on Tregs resulted in increased LFA-1 activation, as measured by increased m-24 mAb staining (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data using m-24 antibody shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Layilin has been shown to bind to collagen IV.
source: Layilin has been shown to bind to collagen IV (Glasgow et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: CRISPR-mediated Layn editing reduces LFA-1 activation only in the presence of collagen IV.
source: Consistent with the results using layilin crosslinking mAbs, these experiments revealed that CRISPR-mediated Layn editing reduces LFA-1 activation only in the presence of collagen IV (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Tregs deficient in layilin displayed a reduced capacity to bind to collagen IV-coated plates but not uncoated plates.
source: Consistent with our previous findings, Tregs deficient in layilin displayed a reduced capacity to bind to collagen IV-coated plates but not uncoated plates (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by adhesion assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Engagement of layilin on Tregs results in enhanced LFA-1 activation and cellular adhesion.
source: Taken together, this data reveals that engagement of layilin on Tregs results in enhanced LFA-1 activation and cellular adhesion.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from multiple experimental approaches including crosslinking, CRISPR editing, and adhesion assays.

claim: Actin polymerization is one of the major cytoskeleton changes involved in cell migration and adhesion.
source: Actin polymerization is one of the major cytoskeleton changes involved in cell migration and adhesion (Gardel et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Layilin-deficient Tregs showed increased F-actin staining and increased cellular projections (consistent with lamellipodia) only in the presence of collagen IV.
source: These experiments revealed increased F-actin staining and increased cellular projections (consistent with lamellipodia) in layilin-deficient cells only in the presence of collagen IV (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by phalloidin staining data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Layilin contains a talin binding domain, which is essential for layilin-LFA-1 interaction in exhausted CD8+ T cells.
source: As previously shown, layilin contains a talin binding domain, which we have shown to be essential for layilin-LFA-1 interaction in exhausted CD8+ T cells (Mahuron et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Talin, vinculin, and paxillin are recruited to form a complex and interact with the binding domain of high-affinity conformation integrins, leading to focal adhesion and slowing cells.
source: Furthermore, talin, vinculin, and paxillin are recruited to form a complex and interact with the binding domain of high-affinity conformation integrins, leading to focal adhesion and slowing cells (Jankowska et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: An increase in polymerized actin content and cellular protrusions correlates with a higher motile profile.
source: Conversely, an increase in polymerized actin content and cellular protrusions correlates with a higher motile profile (Dupré et al., 2015; Yan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Lamellipodia are the main protrusive structures formed by T cells during migration and require actin-related protein 3 (ARP3).
source: Lamellipodia are the main protrusive structures formed by T cells during migration and require actin-related protein 3 (ARP3) (Obeidy et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Layilin, by its interaction with LFA-1 and talin, stabilizes the formation of focal adhesion complexes and favors a more anchored Treg cell phenotype.
source: Taken together, we propose a working model (Figure 5C) in which layilin, by its interaction with LFA-1 and talin, stabilizes the formation of focal adhesion complexes and favors a more anchored Treg cell phenotype.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanistic model based on the experimental data and previous literature.

claim: The absence of layilin promotes cell motility, at least in part, by enhancing lamellipodia formation.
source: Conversely, the absence of layilin promotes cell motility, at least in part, by enhancing lamellipodia formation.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental data showing increased lamellipodia in layilin-deficient cells.

claim: Layilin modulates Treg motility in tissues through the modulation of LFA-1 activation and cytoskeletal remodeling necessary for cellular adhesion and movement.
source: The summation of our data from results presented herein and previous studies (Mehta et al., 2021) suggests that layilin modulates Treg motility in tissues. This effect on motility is mediated, at least in part, through the modulation of LFA-1 activation and contributes to cytoskeletal remodeling necessary for cellular adhesion and movement.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data and previous literature.

claim: Layilin expression is induced on Tregs upon entering non-lymphoid tissues such as skin.
source: Our data supports a model whereby layilin expression is induced on Tregs upon entering non-lymphoid tissues such as skin.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental observations.

claim: Layilin acts to anchor Tregs in the tissue, possibly adjacent to (or within) collagen IV-rich blood vessels.
source: This acts to anchor Tregs in the tissue, possibly adjacent to (or within) collagen IV-rich blood vessels (Uitto et al., 1989; Pfisterer et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental data and previous literature about collagen IV localization.

claim: Layilin may help sequester Tregs to a defined niche, facilitating their ability to maintain tissue immune homeostasis in the steady state.
source: In this capacity, layilin may help sequester Tregs to a defined niche, facilitating their ability to maintain tissue immune homeostasis in the steady state.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the functional role of layilin.

claim: In pathological situations such as tumors and chronic inflammation, the motility of Tregs may play a larger role in their functionality, allowing them to navigate to various tissue microanatomic niches to attenuate specific cell types and inflammatory mediators.
source: Conversely, in pathological situations such as tumors and chronic inflammation, the motility of Tregs may play a larger role in their functionality, allowing them to navigate to various tissue microanatomic niches to attenuate specific cell types and inflammatory mediators.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the role of Treg motility in disease.

claim: Several studies have underscored the crucial role of adhesion properties, particularly those mediated by ICAM-1, in enabling effective Treg suppression capacity.
source: Notably, several studies have underscored the crucial role of adhesion properties, particularly those mediated by ICAM-1, the main adhesion molecule expressed by T cells, in enabling effective Treg suppression capacity (Gottrand et al., 2015; Tran et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Layilin expression on Tregs most likely acts to curtail their suppressive capacity by limiting their motility.
source: In this context, layilin expression on Tregs most likely acts to curtail their suppressive capacity by limiting their motility.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and previous literature.

claim: Two-photon microscopy studies revealed that layilin-deficient Tregs are relatively more motile in inflamed skin compared to layilin-expressing control Tregs.
source: Indeed, two-photon microscopy studies revealed that layilin-deficient Tregs are relatively more motile in inflamed skin compared to layilin-expressing control Tregs (Mehta et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Reducing layilin expression on Tregs results in enhanced immune regulation in a skin inflammation model, as demonstrated by a significant reduction in pro-inflammatory cells.
source: In support of this theory, herein, we show that reducing layilin expression on Tregs results in enhanced immune regulation in a skin inflammation model, as demonstrated by a significant reduction in pro-inflammatory cells, observed in Foxp3Cre/Laynfl/fl mice compared to controls.
evidence: Supported by the IMQ model data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In vitro, layilin plays a minimal role in Treg activation and suppressive capacity.
source: In contrast, it is interesting to highlight that, in vitro, layilin plays a minimal role in Treg activation and suppressive capacity in vitro.
evidence: Supported by the in vitro experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The role of layilin in the suppression capacities of Tregs depends on the more complex, dynamic, and collagen-rich in vivo environment.
source: This suggests the role of layilin in the suppression capacities of Tregs depends on the more complex, dynamic, and collagen-rich in vivo environment.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the contrasting in vitro and in vivo results.

claim: The association between layilin and LFA-1 activation observed in Tregs echoes previous discoveries in CD8+ T cells.
source: An intriguing finding is the association between layilin and LFA-1 activation observed in Tregs, echoing previous discoveries in CD8+ T cells (Mahuron et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous literature findings.

claim: LFA-1 is crucial for T cell engagement at the immune synapse.
source: LFA-1 is crucial for T cell engagement at the immune synapse (Hammer et al., 2019; Franciszkiewicz et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The modulation of LFA-1 by layilin may enhance Treg interactions with other cells, potentially boosting their suppressive abilities, but could also confine their impact to a narrowly defined area due to reduced motility.
source: While the modulation of LFA-1 by layilin may enhance Treg interactions with other cells, potentially boosting their suppressive abilities, it could also confine their impact to a narrowly defined area due to reduced motility.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the dual effects of layilin on Treg function.

claim: Layilin's role in enhancing the effector functions of CD8+ T cells in tumors and limiting Treg-suppressive capacity in inflamed tissues suggests that it could be a valuable therapeutic target for autoimmune and chronic inflammatory diseases.
source: Layilin's role in enhancing the effector functions of CD8+ T cells in tumors (Zheng et al., 2017; Mahuron et al., 2020; Pan et al., 2019) and limiting Treg-suppressive capacity in inflamed tissues suggests that it could be a valuable therapeutic target for autoimmune and chronic inflammatory diseases.
evidence: This is a speculative therapeutic hypothesis based on the experimental data and previous literature.

claim: A layilin neutralizing antibody could attenuate CD8+ T cell killing and enhance Treg suppression, effectively working in concert to dampen tissue inflammation.
source: A layilin neutralizing antibody could attenuate CD8+ T cell killing and enhance Treg suppression, effectively working in concert to dampen tissue inflammation.
evidence: This is a speculative therapeutic hypothesis.

claim: Tissue-specific autoimmune diseases thought to be mediated by autoreactive CD8+ T cells and suboptimally controlled by Tregs would be attractive indications for layilin-targeted therapy.
source: Tissue-specific autoimmune diseases thought to be mediated by autoreactive CD8+ T cells and suboptimally controlled by Tregs would be attractive indications.
evidence: This is a speculative therapeutic hypothesis.

claim: More research is necessary to understand the role of layilin on non-immune cells, such as gastrointestinal epithelial cells, to help build confidence around the therapeutic hypothesis.
source: However, more research is necessary to understand the role of layilin on non-immune cells, such as gastrointestinal epithelial cells (Bono et al., 2001; Kim et al., 2018), to help build confidence around this therapeutic hypothesis.
evidence: This acknowledges limitations and the need for further research, with citations to previous work on layilin in non-immune cells.
